18428-the-feast-at-solhoug:
Henrik Ibsen wrote The Feast at Solhoug in Bergen in the summer of 1855. It was first acted on January 2, 1856, as a gala piece for the anniversary of the Norwegian stage. Ibsen, then stage manager of the Bergen Theatre, conducted the rehearsals himself. William Archer and Mary Morrison translated the play for Archer's collected Ibsen, volume one, with an introduction on its history.

The introduction notes that the play followed Lady Inger of Ostrat by exactly a year, and quotes George Brandes on the charm of old ballad metre for Scandinavian ears. Ibsen answered his critics in a preface to the second edition. Readers get an early Ibsen drama in ballad spirit: a medieval Norwegian feast, love, and honor, told in verse that keeps the music of the old songs.
18719-space-tug:
Murray Leinster published this science fiction novel in 1953 with Shasta, reprinted by Pocket Books in 1955. It is a sequel to his Space Platform, following Joe Kenmore and his crew. The book opens in terror: locked out of the Space Platform, Joe and Haney float outside with only thirty minutes of oxygen left, four thousand miles above Earth.

How they win back inside, and what work their tug must do in orbit, drives the tale. Leinster, a veteran of the field, writes hard, practical space adventure with tools, air, and nerve at the fore. The novel is a brisk classic of early space fiction.
20097-the-tale-of-mrs-ladybug:
Arthur Scott Bailey published The Tale of Mrs. Ladybug in 1921, a children's nature tale. Mrs. Ladybug lives in Pleasant Valley and works hard each day. No one helps Farmer Green more than she does, the book says. She works to keep his orchard trees free from harmful insects.

Yet she also loves a bit of gossip with her neighbours. That mix of work and chat makes her a warm, funny figure. Bailey's tales teach real animal facts inside small, bright stories. Young readers learn why ladybugs help farms while they follow her daily rounds.
21939-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-44:
A sultan and his clever bear open this number of Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, dated Saturday, August 7, 1852, price three halfpence. William and Robert Chambers conducted the weekly, famous for cheap, improving reading for the people. In The Sultan's Bear, a Jewish physician humors his royal patient by praising the bear at his feet. The sultan swears the beast has gathered knowledge and uses it with logical correctness.

The tale turns on flattery and what a courtier dares to say. Around it, the journal fills its pages with the usual mix of story, fact, and moral piece. Chambers's reached readers who could afford little else. One weekly number shows Victorian self-education at work: bright, brief, and priced for a workman's pocket.
22161-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-45:
Chambers's Edinburgh Journal was the Chambers brothers' cheap weekly for self-improving readers. Number 450, new series, appeared on Saturday, August 14, 1852, at three halfpence. Its leading article weighs the useful-knowledge movement. The writer grants that science needs exact description, down to the markings of a shell, but denies that every reader must follow the minutiae.

Stories, essays, poems, and facts fill the rest of the number. William and Robert Chambers built their publishing house on such improving fare at low prices. The journal carried knowledge into cottages and workshops across Britain. One issue shows the whole machine: useful, respectable, and quietly ambitious for its readers.
22178-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-45:
Number 451 of Chambers's Edinburgh Journal appeared on Saturday, August 21, 1852. The Chambers brothers' weekly cost three halfpence and aimed at every literate household. Its lead article asks "Who shall rule the waves?" A remarkable contest at sea is under way, the writer says, and Brother Jonathan has thrown down the gauntlet to the Britishers.

The contest is yacht racing: America's schooner had beaten Britain's fleet the year before. Around the lead sit stories, including a tale of a girl told her dead father's wish about her marriage. Facts, fiction, and improvement share the pages as usual. The number catches Britain mid-century, proud, curious, and stung by American speed.
22187-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-45:
Chambers's Edinburgh Journal number 452 appeared on Saturday, August 28, 1852. The Chambers brothers priced their weekly at three halfpence for the widest reach. Its pages carry a serial tale of Frances, a girl about to come out in society. Her guardian, Mrs. Wentworth, must tell her of a wish in her dead father's letter, touching her choice of a husband.

Essays, facts, and shorter pieces surround the fiction as the journal's readers expected. The Chambers formula joined improvement to entertainment without sermons. By 1852 the paper was a fixture of respectable households across the empire. This issue is a typical brick from that edifice of cheap, improving print.
29480-hymns-from-the-morningland-being-t:
John Brownlie, D.D., gathered these hymns in 1911 from the service books of the Eastern Church, in translations, centos, and fresh suggestions of his own. Paisley publisher Alexander Gardner printed the sixth series, with a London issue from Simpkin, Marshall. Brownlie, already known for hymns of the Greek Church, here turns Eastern liturgy into English verse for church use.

The hymns follow the church year: morning praise, glory to God, the risen Christ, and the Ascension borne on clouds. Their lines are short, plain, and made for singing, not for show. Readers who love hymns, liturgy, or Eastern Christian worship will find a devout, musical book that opens a distant rite to English tongues.
33030-chiquita-an-american-novel-the-rom:
Merrill Tileston's Chiquita, an American novel published in Chicago in 1902, tells the romance of a Ute chief's daughter. Its chapters run from a Bozrah bornin and the firing line of civilization through cats, traps, and Indians, old Joe Riggs, and a camp in the willows. They go on to a ranch on the Troublesome, Chiquita wooed by Antelope, and a glimpse of home. Later chapters bring the Blazing Eye mine, college vacations, Estes Park, and Chiquita's graduation.

The novel follows its heroine between two worlds, Ute life and the schools, hospitals, and boarding houses of white civilization, asking where her people come from and where she belongs. Tileston writes in the popular manner of the day, with adventure, sentiment, and local color. Modern readers will note its period attitudes, but the story's sweep, from frontier camp to college, still gives it a strong pull.
5980-kent-knowles-quahaug:
Joseph C. Lincoln tells a Cape Cod tale whose chapters tease rather than tell, promising family history, a sail with Hephzy aboard the Plutonia, and a stay at Bancroft's Hotel. The narrator repeats what Jim Campbell said to him, mingles with the upper classes, and finds a dream becoming real.

Pilgrims become tenants, Mayberry and a stretch of Burgleston Bogs appear, and complications grow more complicated until truth is told at last. Golf, a channel crossing, abbeys that are not churches, and a turn as invalid fill the later pages. The pilgrimage ends where it began, among quahaugs.
britannica-1911-jug:
A jug is a vessel for holding liquid, most often with one handle and a lip, made of earthenware, glass, or metal. The origin of the word is unsure, but it is most likely a short form of the woman's name Joan or Joanna. Jack and Jill were used the same way for drink vessels.

The word has also served as a plain term for a servant girl or a sweetheart, and in slang a stone jug means a prison. Used of sound, it copies a note in the nightingale's song. The entry then lingers on one fine piece: a bronze jug in the British Museum, found at Kumasi during the Ashanti expedition of 1896. It dates from the reign of Richard II and bears the arms of England and the king's badge in relief. Bands round its body carry a rhyming warning against waste.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hug:
Johann Leonhard Hug was a German Catholic exegete, born at Constance in 1765 and dead at Freiburg in 1846. After school in his native town he entered Freiburg University in 1783. He was ordained in 1789, and became professor of Old Testament exegesis in 1791, adding the New Testament chair a year later. His chief works include studies of the Vatican Codex, an introduction to the New Testament, and commentaries on the Song of Songs and the Alexandrine Pentateuch.

Hug was an independent thinker and keen student who went to the roots of things. He entered the critics' camp fearlessly, treating New Testament problems from a historical standpoint and striking hard at subjective criticism from its own ground. His method demanded that conjectures rest on historical facts from the New Testament or other study, and his report on Strauss's Life of Jesus closed his major work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julius-von-pf:
Julius von Pflug was the last Catholic bishop of Naumburg-Zeitz, as Lutheran teaching spread through Saxony. Born at Eythra in 1499, he studied at Leipzig, Padua, and Bologna, where he took a doctorate in laws in 1521. A humanist and a diplomat by gift, he favored peace and was willing to give ground even on doctrine and discipline. His presence was therefore requested at nearly every conference that sought common ground between Catholics and Evangelicals.

He took part in the Leipzig discussions of 1534 and in later efforts under the Bishop of Meissen, without pacifying either side. The chapter chose him as bishop in January 1541, fearing the elector would fill the vacancy himself. The elector's hostility followed him, but Pflug kept his see until his death at Zeitz in 1564. He was a conciliator caught between a reforming prince and a chapter determined to elect its own bishop.
doe-osti-3375875-identifying-the-accurac:
National Energy Technology Laboratory report DOE/NETL-2026/5329, dated January 21, 2026, tests how well CT scanning measures surface roughness on printed metal parts. Four authors share it: Owen Grabowski, Bryan Hughes, Shane Namie, and Douglas Straub, who led the work. Roughness drives how a part wears and cracks, so builders need it right. A CT scan can read inner and outer faces at once. The catch is that scan flaws may warp the very texture being read.

The test piece was a ribbed block, scanned and rebuilt in three dimensions. The team fit a curved mean plane to the face of interest. They then flagged bad slices at the head and tail of each scan. Early and late slices showed part-frame shadows and jumps in brightness. Final slices streaked and warped at the edges. Those flaws track start-up flux swings and detector overload in thick parts.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-in: This file, dated August 1998, sits in the Federal Bureau of Investigation interview records later drawn on for the September 11 commission work. The text layer that survives here is almost wholly garbled. Letters and word forms are scrambled past the point where names, places, or statements can be read with trust. What can be said is plain: the bureau kept an interview record from that month, held with the wider set of interview papers. No claim about who was spoken to, or what was said, can rest on these pages.

Samuel G. Coombs came forward of his own will in this Federal Bureau of Investigation interview record from August 2002. He kept a set time with an agent at the Macomb County office in Michigan. Agents from the New York division spoke with him by phone. The talk took place on August 21, 2002, and the report was dictated days later. The file as freed is short and thick with withheld blocks. It proves the meeting and its date. What Coombs told the agents is not legible here.

August 1999 in this file is a second send of the July 8, 1999, cable on the Manila Air case, kept by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. New York sent the sum of the case to security staff and to posts across Asia. In January 1996, the cable says, a fresh plotter was named: Khalid Shaikh Mohammad.

The pages give his life in brief. He was born in Kuwait in 1965 and stayed through secondary school. In 1984 he went to the United States and earned a degree in mechanical engineering. Work in Kuwait did not come, so he left for Peshawar, in Pakistan, and joined an Afghan party led by Abdul Rasul Sayyaf. By 1992 he was in Qatar, in a job the cable begins to describe as the sample ends.

August 2002 papers in this Federal Bureau of Investigation file mix an Al Qaeda primer with phone record checks. The head pages are garbled in the text layer. The body, though, can be read in part, and it ties a Virginia phone number to the hijackers' last days.

The records concern a number at Falls Church, Virginia. The file notes that four known hijackers came to see the man who held it. A call dated September 10, 2001, is picked out for note. Other pages trace who a phone in Arlington was signed up to, and who the bureau spoke to about the numbers. Names and most numbers are masked. What stands is the method: after the attacks, the bureau rebuilt the plot one phone bill at a time.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-th:
August 2001 pages from the daily threat update close this set of Federal Bureau of Investigation warning files. The update was kept by the Usama Bin Laden and Radical Fundamentalist unit. Its note to readers calls the text raw reporting, held back from case files and from wide spread.

The sampled pages strike a careful tone. One item says a piece of reporting is likely bogus. The bureau still sent word out, it explains, because the threat from Bin Laden and his backers went on. A second note warns that much of the threat word in past updates had been dressed up or made up by its sources. The file is a study in doubt: warnings the bureau felt it must pass on, from sources it did not fully trust.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-McHughGodfreyBr:
Dorothy McCardle's 'People' column in the Washington Post, dated May 6, 1974, was titled 'Talk of the Tapes.' Its subject was Senator Sam Ervin of North Carolina. Ervin chaired the Senate committee investigating Watergate. McCardle describes his deep immersion in reading about the scandal that spring.

A society-page column is an odd place for Watergate, which is part of the interest. The column treats the tapes fight as Washington talk, measured in one man's reading habits. The item was filed under the name of Brigadier General Godfrey McHugh, a former Kennedy aide. That filing choice shows how a researcher's clippings were sorted: by person, whatever the page contained.
kent-knowles-quahaug:
Kent Knowles: Quahaug is a novel by Joseph C. Lincoln, published in 1914. Eighteen chapters tell how Kent Knowles and his friend Hephzy leave their Cape Cod town by ship. They sail on the Plutonia, stay at Bancroft's Hotel, and become tenants in an English village. Husbands, wives, and sweethearts get a chapter of their own.

Kent loses three pounds, finds Mayberry, and writes home about his good luck. A visit to Burgleston Bogs, a day of golf, and a channel crossing fill the middle. In chapter twelve somebody tells Kent the truth, and Hephzy outfaces an English woman. A surprise from Solomon Cripps and a parting close the book. Lincoln writes his Cape Codders abroad with dry, affectionate humor.
podcast-tuckercarlson-4K1nnOXKrUg:
Tucker Carlson argues in this episode that President Joe Biden's campaign amounts to a campaign against Christianity itself. The case rests on the administration's positions, prosecutions, and public statements, which Carlson reads as a pattern of hostility toward traditional Christian belief and practice in America.

Rather than a guest interview, the episode is driven by Carlson's own narration of events he treats as connected. Religious liberty lawyers would call several of his examples live legal fights; his critics would call the pattern cherry-picked. Either way, the recording captures how a leading conservative broadcaster framed the 2024-era culture war for his audience: faith under pressure from the state, with an election cast as the remedy. It stands as his argument, in his words.
space-tug:
Murray Leinster opens Space Tug with thirty minutes to live. Joe Kenmore hears the airlock close with a wheeze and a clank and turns to Haney in despair. Through the clear domes of their helmets, horror and unbelief cross Haney's face. The crew is locked out of the Space Platform, with the Earth circling four thousand miles below and the steel hull of their home under their feet.

Without tools there is no hope of getting back inside, and Joe's oxygen meter reads thirty minutes. A note on the book calls Space Tug a free-standing sequel to Leinster's Space Platform. Both books were first printed by Shasta Publishers. Other Leinster titles on the page name Sidewise in Time, Murder Madness, and The Last Space Ship.
the-feast-at-solhoug:
Henrik Ibsen wrote The Feast at Solhoug early in his career, and William Archer and Mary Morrison turned it into English. Archer's introduction tells how the play first reached the stage at Bergen.

Archer notes that the play came out a year after Lady Inger of Ostrat, on the Bergen Theatre's foundation day. Its verse owes much to old heroic ballads, with their swing and rich tone. Critic George Brandes is quoted on that debt and on Hertz's Svend Dyring's House as a model. The young Ibsen built a tale of love and feud in the dress and music of Norway's past.
